strengths: Significance: Reducing edge-feature materialization is a useful objective for atomistic models. Combining node-wise geometric factorization with sparse streaming attention could substantially improve practical scalability.

Originality: Integrating E2Former’s Wigner-6j factorization, axis-aligned SO(2) operations, and GPU kernel fusion is a potentially valuable systems contribution, although the individual ingredients are established.

Empirical merits: Figure 4 reports substantial throughput and memory improvements over a naive PyTorch implementation. Table 3 reports inference at 100,000 atoms for both direct and conservative variants, while Tables 1–2 show useful predictive accuracy across two molecular benchmarks.

Presentation: The source preparation, aggregation, and target coupling decomposition is understandable. Algorithm 1 clearly describes online softmax accumulation, and separating direct from conservative force prediction is appropriate.
weaknesses: Soundness—exactness is not established by the stated mathematics. Proposition 4.3 omits the nonzero pole value of the solid spherical harmonic, including its radial factor ||r||^ell_f. Scaling r changes the left side of Eq. (14), while the defined right side depends only on its direction. Appendix B repeats this omission rather than resolving it. Moreover, C is explicitly defined as the real-basis CG coefficient, yet Eq. (13) multiplies its surviving odd-parity entry by an additional -2(-1)^m without a convincing derivation. Correct identities and numerical equivalence/gradient checks are needed to support the central exactness claim.

Soundness—implementation evidence conflicts with the central memory claim. Appendix A’s 'Ours' code explicitly constructs scores of shape N×K×H, applies a separate softmax, and passes alpha to another kernel. This is not the fully fused online algorithm described in Section 4.4. The manuscript must identify which implementation produced each result. Only forward pseudocode is supplied; backward execution, saved activations, and higher-order differentiation needed for conservative-force training are not documented or benchmarked.

Efficiency comparisons do not adequately establish the claimed advantage. Figure 1’s 'Traditional EGNNs' is a generic gather-based attention implementation, rather than an actual EGNN, and its 'FlashAttention' baseline is masked PyTorch SDPA without verification of the selected backend or sparse execution. Table 3 lacks sufficiently specified model configurations and precision settings. Appendix D says all runs use torch.no_grad() despite conservative forces requiring differentiation, without explaining any internal gradient re-enabling. It also labels other runtime failures as OOM, undermining the memory-limit conclusions.

Predictive-performance claims conflict with the tables. Section 5.3 states that the conservative OMol25 model achieves aggregate energy MAE 1.27, matching eSEN-small; Table 2 reports 2.09 for E2V2-Cons and 1.27 for eSEN-sm-cons. On SPICE, eSEN-Cons achieves 0.23/6.36 aggregate energy/force MAE, versus 0.57/7.80 for E2V2-Cons, and E2Former-V1 also has lower aggregate force error. These results support a possible efficiency–accuracy tradeoff, not the broad claims of superior predictive performance.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The abstract ends with an empty code-availability statement. The manuscript omits essential model sizes, layer configurations, optimizer and schedule settings, training budgets, loss weights, dataset versions/splits, and baseline training provenance. Kernel dimensions and implementation details are also incomplete. Without these, neither accuracy nor matched-cost efficiency can be independently assessed.

Significance and originality are overstated relative to the evidence. With bounded neighbor count, the paper itself acknowledges that existing O(|E|)=O(NK) activation memory is already linear in N; the meaningful benefit is reduced neighbor-dependent intermediate storage, not an unconditional transition from nonlinear to linear scaling. The neighbor index still occupies O(NK) memory. The evaluation lacks full-model ablations isolating EAAS and fusion, comparisons against existing SO(2) implementations for the algebraic component, and training-throughput measurements supporting the training-efficiency claims.

Limitations and physical validation need substantially better treatment. The water RDF experiment omits temperature, ensemble, timestep, trajectory duration, equilibration, uncertainty, and the experimental reference source; it cannot establish the claimed long-term dynamical fidelity. Numerical stability under translations of absolute-coordinate solid harmonics and periodic-boundary handling are also unresolved, especially since Appendix D disables PBC. No material research-ethics concern is apparent, but the absence of a substantive limitations discussion leaves these practical boundaries unclear.

strengths: Significance: Reducing intermediate memory and execution overhead in equivariant atomistic models is a useful research goal. Combining node-wise geometric factorization with sparse attention kernels could provide substantial practical benefits.

Originality: Integrating E2Former’s Wigner-6j factorization, axis-aligned tensor products, and streaming attention is a potentially valuable systems contribution. Novelty can reside in making these components work efficiently together, even though the individual principles have precedents.

Empirical merits: The reported results show promising accuracy and throughput. E2V2-Direct achieves the lowest aggregate energy error in Table 2, while Table 3 reports operation at 100,000 atoms for both variants. Separating direct and conservative force prediction is helpful.

Presentation: The source preparation, aggregation, and target coupling decomposition provides an accessible architectural overview. Algorithm 1 clearly describes the intended online softmax computation, and the appendices provide some useful timing and synthetic-system details.
weaknesses: Soundness—exactness of EAAS is not established as written. Equation (14) equates a tensor product with solid spherical harmonics to an operator containing only fixed Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and rotations. The pole amplitude, including the radius-dependent factor ||r||^ell_f from Equation (2), is absent. Scaling r therefore changes the left-hand side but not the right-hand side. Appendix B repeats this omission. Its additional odd-parity factor also requires a consistent derivation, since C is already defined as the real-basis coefficient. These are material problems for a central exact-equivalence claim; numerical comparisons of outputs and derivatives against the original tensor product are needed.

Soundness—the implementation evidence contradicts the central fusion claim. Section 4.4 and Algorithm 1 state that scores and attention weights are never materialized, but Appendix A’s proposed implementation explicitly creates scores of shape N × K × H, applies a separate softmax, and passes alpha to another kernel. Although this can avoid much larger gathered feature tensors, it does not demonstrate the advertised elimination of edge-level attention activations. The paper must identify which implementation produced each result.

Training scalability is insufficiently supported. Only a forward streaming algorithm is provided, without the backward/recomputation implementation, gradient validation, or measured training throughput and memory. Conservative-force training additionally requires differentiating through energy gradients. The introduction’s training-efficiency claims cannot be established from forward microbenchmarks and inference results. Moreover, fixed-degree baselines already have O(KN) = O(N) activation scaling; the claimed benefit needs to distinguish reduced dependence on K and feature dimensions from asymptotic scaling in N.

Efficiency comparisons do not adequately establish the claimed advantage over optimized alternatives. Figure 1’s 'Traditional EGNNs' curve is a synthetic gather-based attention implementation, rather than an evaluated EGNN architecture. Its 'FlashAttention' curve uses masked PyTorch SDPA without specifying or verifying the selected backend; a dense masked operation also differs computationally from sparse neighbor attention. Figure 4 compares against naive PyTorch, without sufficient configuration or profiling evidence to establish a compute-bound regime. The conclusion further presents a roughly 20× kernel result as an inference speedup.

Reproducibility is substantially incomplete. The abstract’s code-release statement has no URL, and the paper omits essential architecture sizes, training schedules, optimizer and loss settings, dataset versions/splits, and baseline checkpoint details. Appendix D says all inference runs use torch.no_grad() despite benchmarking energy-gradient forces; any internal gradient re-enabling must be specified. It also labels other runtime errors as OOM, undermining interpretation of the memory-scaling comparison.

Presentation and evidential accuracy: Section 5.3 attributes an OMol25 aggregate energy MAE of 1.27 to E2V2-Cons, whereas Table 2 reports 2.09; 1.27 belongs to eSEN. On SPICE, eSEN-Cons has substantially better aggregate energy/force errors (0.23/6.36) than either proposed variant. Competitive performance is plausible, but the broad superiority claims overstate the tables. Matched accuracy–runtime comparisons and component ablations are also missing.

Limitations and physical validation are underdeveloped. Figure 5 supplies one water RDF without simulation duration, temperature, ensemble, timestep, uncertainty, or an identifiable experimental reference. This does not establish long-term dynamical fidelity. The use of absolute-coordinate solid harmonics also warrants translation and numerical-stability checks, and the large-system benchmark disables periodic boundaries. No specific research-ethics violation is apparent, but these practical limitations should be assessed before claiming broad suitability for molecular simulation.

strengths: Significance: Reducing intermediate memory in equivariant molecular models is a useful practical goal. Combining node-based factorization with sparse GPU execution could enable substantially larger atomistic calculations.

Originality: Integrating E2Former’s Wigner-6j factorization, SO(2) sparsification, and streaming attention is a potentially valuable systems contribution, even though the individual principles build on established work.

Empirical merits: Table 3 reports substantial throughput improvements and execution at 100,000 atoms in both force-prediction settings. SPICE results show improvements over E2Former-V1 on several subsets, and evaluation covers two substantial molecular datasets.

Presentation: Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 make the intended computational pipeline understandable. Separating conservative and direct-force throughput is appropriate. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—exactness is not established by the stated derivation. Proposition 4.3 equates a tensor product involving solid harmonics with a rotation and the operator P, but P in Eq. (13) omits the geometric amplitude R^(ℓf)_0 in the aligned frame. Scaling r changes the left-hand side by its radial degree while leaving the stated right-hand side unchanged. Appendix B likewise drops this factor. Moreover, Eqs. (8)–(10) do not specify how the sums, signs, and recoupling coefficients in Eq. (5) are implemented. These omissions require corrected formulas and numerical equivalence and symmetry checks.

Soundness—the implementation evidence contradicts the central fusion claim. Section 4.4 describes online softmax without materialized scores, whereas Appendix A explicitly creates scores and alpha of shape N × K × H between separate kernels. This still avoids large gathered feature tensors, but does not demonstrate the advertised elimination of edge-dependent attention activations. Only a forward algorithm is provided; the backward/recomputation scheme and training-memory measurements needed to substantiate the training claims are absent.

Complexity claims need qualification. At fixed neighbor count, conventional O(NK) edge activations are already linear in N, and the proposed method retains an N × K neighbor-index tensor and performs work per interaction. The meaningful benefit is reduced intermediate storage and memory traffic; the manuscript repeatedly conflates this with eliminating edge complexity.

Evaluation—baseline definitions and timing details weaken the efficiency conclusions. Figure 1 labels an explicit-gather PyTorch attention sketch as 'Traditional EGNNs' and masked scaled_dot_product_attention as 'FlashAttention' without establishing the actual backend or comparable sparse execution. Appendix D marks other runtime errors as OOM and states that all runs use torch.no_grad(), leaving conservative-force differentiation unexplained unless gradients are explicitly re-enabled internally. Model configurations and matched accuracy–throughput comparisons are also missing. Kernel TFLOPS improvements alone do not establish the claimed transition to compute-bound execution.

Presentation and evidential accuracy: Section 5.3 says the conservative OMol25 model achieves aggregate energy MAE 1.27, matching eSEN; Table 2 instead reports 2.09 for E2V2-Cons. and 1.27 for eSEN. On SPICE, eSEN-Cons. has better aggregate energy and force errors than either proposed variant. The conclusion’s claims of superior predictive performance and 20× inference acceleration therefore exceed what the reported model-level comparisons establish.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a contribution centered on implementation. The abstract’s code-availability statement has no link, and the manuscript omits essential architecture sizes, optimization settings, training budgets, dataset splits, and baseline configurations. There is no controlled end-to-end ablation separating EAAS from attention fusion, nor sufficient kernel configuration and backward-pass detail to reproduce the main results.

Limitations and physical validation are insufficiently developed. The water RDF experiment lacks temperature, ensemble, timestep, trajectory duration, uncertainty, and an identifiable experimental reference; it cannot establish long-term dynamics fidelity by itself. The manuscript also does not assess numerical stability of the absolute-coordinate factorization or delimit the implications of benchmarking large systems with periodic boundaries disabled. These are unresolved validation gaps, rather than reasons to discount an otherwise honest limitations discussion.

strengths: Significance: Reducing edge-feature materialization addresses a practical bottleneck in equivariant atomistic models. Table 5 reports useful gains, including conservative inference at 100k atoms at 0.12 steps/s versus 0.04 for UMA-S.

Empirical merits: The evaluation includes SPICE, OMol25, OC20, optimized tensor-product libraries, and component ablations. Table 4 separates the contributions of fusion and EAAS, with combined throughput increasing from 1.40 to 4.24 samples/s at 5k atoms.

Predictive performance: The reported accuracy is competitive. On OMol25, the conservative model achieves 1.16 meV/atom energy MAE and 8.38 meV/Å force MAE, compared with 1.27 and 8.25 for eSEN-small-conservative.

Originality and presentation: Combining node-factorized equivariant operations with sparse streaming attention is a potentially useful systems contribution. The pipeline illustration and online-softmax pseudocode communicate the intended design clearly.

Limitations and ethics: The appendices acknowledge reduced advantages for very sparse graphs, an expressivity trade-off, and lower arithmetic throughput than dense attention. These are useful qualifications. The impact statement appropriately acknowledges general molecular-design dual-use risks; no specific material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central implementation contradiction: Section 4.4 and Algorithm 1 describe fully fused online softmax without materialized edge scores. However, Appendix A's implementation explicitly creates scores and alpha of shape N×K×H through separate QK, softmax, and value kernels. This retains edge-dependent activations and leaves unclear which implementation produced the results. A forward-only algorithm also does not establish the claimed training-memory behavior; backward and higher-order differentiation for conservative force training are not described.

Soundness—incorrect exact identity as written: Proposition 4.3 omits the surviving geometric factor R^(ℓf)_0(Rr), including its radius dependence. Equations (13)–(14) depend on direction through rotations but cannot reproduce the ||r||^ℓf scaling defined in Equation (2). Appendix C repeats this omission. Its additional odd-parity multiplier is also unexplained given that C is already defined as the real-basis CG coefficient. Correct identities and numerical equivalence/gradient checks are needed to support theoretical exactness.

Soundness—unclear evaluated architecture: Equations (6)–(7) construct invariant scalar attention, whereas Appendix D identifies the implemented configuration with a different score involving a nonlinear edge feature. The componentwise product and pointwise nonlinearity on higher-order representations in Equation (34) are not generally equivariant, and the manuscript does not specify an invariant contraction resolving this issue. Algorithm 1 also omits this feature. Consequently, the accuracy results cannot be confidently linked to the analyzed equivariant kernel.

Efficiency evidence and presentation: Figure 1 labels a synthetic gather/softmax microbenchmark as 'Traditional EGNNs' and masked PyTorch SDPA as 'FlashAttention', without establishing the dispatched backend. Appendix H marks other runtime errors as OOM and states that all runs use torch.no_grad(), without explaining how conservative energy gradients are enabled. Table 10 specifies at most 32 neighbors, while throughput discussions use approximately 50; matched neighbor budgets and baseline configurations are insufficiently documented. These ambiguities materially weaken the claimed comparisons.

Complexity and originality: At bounded degree, O(Nk) is already linear in N; the practical advance is reducing edge-dependent storage and constants. Neighbor-list storage remains O(Nk), and Appendix J incorrectly suggests an asymptotic memory advantage over dense FlashAttention after listing both fused methods as O(N) memory. The algebraic novelty beyond E2Former's factorization and established SO(2) alignment is insufficiently isolated.

Reproducibility and accuracy attribution: The abstract's promised code link is blank. Dataset versions and splits, baseline training budgets, checkpoint selection, and complete kernel details are insufficiently specified. Appendix I describes extensive OMol25 pretraining and additional conservative training, but equivalent baseline data exposure is not established. SPICE aggregate results also favor eSEN-conservative over the proposed model, so claims of superior accuracy require qualification.

Physical validation: Figure 4 provides a water RDF and one protein trajectory, but omits essential reproduction details such as protein identity, experimental RDF source, integration timestep, thermostat settings, and uncertainty across runs. A fluctuating high TM-score supports stability of that trajectory, not a general protein-refinement claim. No energy-drift assessment or explanation of periodic-image handling in the absolute-coordinate factorization is provided.

strengths: Significance: Reducing edge-feature materialization is a useful systems objective for atomistic models. Combining node-level geometric factorization with sparse attention fusion could substantially improve practical scalability.

Empirical merits: Table 4 provides a useful component ablation: at 5,000 atoms, throughput increases from 1.40 to 4.24 samples/s, with the fused kernel contributing most of the gain. Table 3 includes optimized tensor-product libraries rather than only an unoptimized reference.

Predictive performance: The reported SPICE and OMol25 results are competitive. For example, the conservative model achieves SPICE energy/force MAEs of 0.31/7.05 versus 0.23/6.36 for conservative eSEN, suggesting a potentially useful accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

Presentation and limitations: The overall architectural motivation is understandable, and Appendices D and E acknowledge expressivity trade-offs and reduced benefits on very sparse graphs. The impact statement acknowledges general molecular-design dual-use risks; no specific unresolved ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—exact algebraic equivalence is not established as written. Equation (14) equates a tensor product with solid spherical harmonics to rotations and the fixed operator P, but omits the surviving pole amplitude, proportional to ||r||^ell_f. Scaling r therefore changes the left-hand side without changing the stated right-hand side. Appendix C repeats this omission. Moreover, C is explicitly defined as the real-basis CG coefficient, yet the odd-parity branch adds a factor -2(-1)^m whose consistency with the original contraction is not demonstrated. Corrected identities and numerical tensor-product/gradient equivalence tests are needed.

Soundness—the evaluated attention mechanism is ambiguous. Equations (7) and (18) use invariant node queries/keys and a radial bias, whereas Appendix D says the reported configuration additionally uses the edge feature in Equations (34)–(35). A componentwise product and pointwise nonlinearity on higher-order irreps do not generally produce an invariant scalar, and the required contraction is unspecified. Thus the main-text equivariance argument does not establish equivariance of the stated experimental configuration.

The central memory claim conflicts with the supplied implementation sketch. Algorithm 1 streams scores and normalization without storing edge attention, but Appendix A explicitly constructs scores and alpha of shape N × K × H using separate kernels and softmax. This still avoids large gathered value tensors, but does not establish the claimed elimination of edge activations. No backward algorithm or training-memory measurements establish the corresponding training claim. Also, for fixed bounded K, both O(NK) and O(N) are linear in N; the distinction should be framed precisely in terms of dependence on K and feature dimensions.

Efficiency comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Figure 1 labels a generic PyTorch sparse-attention implementation 'Traditional EGNNs' and masked SDPA 'FlashAttention,' without identifying the selected SDPA backend. These labels overstate what is compared. Appendix H groups unrelated runtime failures with genuine OOM failures and states that all runs use torch.no_grad(), without explaining how conservative force gradients are enabled. Table 10 specifies at most 32 neighbors, whereas the throughput discussion uses approximately 50; matched neighbor budgets and model configurations need clarification. The conclusion also generalizes the approximately 20× kernel result into an inference-speed claim.

Reproducibility and accuracy comparisons remain incomplete. The abstract's code-release statement has no URL. Although training hyperparameters are provided, exact SPICE versions/splits, baseline checkpoints and training histories, and custom-kernel backward details are missing. Appendix I describes OMol25 pretraining and SPICE fine-tuning, including further training for the conservative model, without establishing comparable baseline data exposure or clearly identifying the checkpoints evaluated on OMol25. Section 5.1 also reports an OMol25 conservative energy MAE of 1.27, while Table 2 reports 1.16.

The physical-fidelity claims exceed the evidence. One water RDF and one protein TM-score trajectory support limited structural plausibility, but do not establish accurate long-time dynamics or reliable protein refinement. The protein identity, experimental reference, simulation timestep, thermostat details, water equilibration/sampling protocol, experimental RDF source, and replicate uncertainty are not supplied. A high TM-score alone does not demonstrate improvement over the starting structure or a suitable simulation baseline.

Originality: The potentially distinctive contribution is the integration and execution strategy. Node-centric factorization is inherited from E2Former, axis alignment from prior SO(2) methods, and online softmax from FlashAttention. This combination could justify acceptance, but the manuscript needs to isolate its new algebraic content and substantiate its implementation. The unresolved correctness and evaluation issues currently prevent reliable reuse.

strengths: Significance: Reducing edge-feature materialization is a useful systems contribution for atomistic models. Table 4 provides encouraging component ablations: throughput at 5,000 atoms increases from 1.40 to 4.24 samples/s, and the fused kernel enables the reported 10,000-atom runs.

Empirical merits: The reported accuracy is competitive across SPICE, OMol25, and OC20. Table 2 reports conservative OMol25 errors of 1.16 meV/atom and 8.38 meV/Å, versus 1.27 and 8.25 for eSEN-small-conservative. Table 3 also includes optimized equivariant libraries rather than only a naive baseline.

Originality: Combining E2Former’s node factorization with axis-aligned sparse operations and streaming sparse attention is a potentially valuable integration of algebra and GPU execution, even though the underlying ingredients have precedents.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture diagram, online-softmax pseudocode, component ablation, and training tables help explain the approach. Appendix E appropriately acknowledges that node-level overhead can make the method slower on very sparse graphs. The impact statement acknowledges molecular-design dual use; no specific unresolved ethical issue is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—exactness is not established as written. Proposition 4.3 omits the aligned harmonic amplitude R^(ℓf)_0(Rr), which includes the radius-dependent factor ||r||^ℓf. The operator P in Eq. (13) contains only CG coefficients and features, so its right-hand side cannot reproduce the claimed tensor product when the radius changes. Appendix C repeats this omission. It also introduces an additional odd-parity multiplier despite defining C as the real-basis CG coefficient, without an explicit calculation establishing that normalization. Corrected identities and numerical equivalence tests are necessary.

Soundness—the evaluated attention mechanism is ambiguous. Equations (6)–(7) and Algorithm 1 use invariant node queries/keys and a distance-only bias. Appendix D instead identifies the trained configuration with an additional nonlinear edge feature in Eqs. (34)–(35). Its dimensions and invariant contraction are unspecified; pointwise nonlinearities on non-scalar irreps do not generally preserve equivariance. The paper must reconcile these formulations and explain how the actual edge computation fits the proposed kernel.

Soundness and reproducibility—the implementation evidence conflicts with the central fusion claim. Appendix A’s implementation explicitly returns an N×K×H score tensor, applies a separate softmax, and invokes a second value kernel. That is different from Algorithm 1’s fully fused online reduction. Only forward pseudocode is provided, leaving backward execution, conservative-force differentiation, and training activation memory insufficiently established.

Benchmark validity: Appendix H labels both memory failures and other runtime errors as OOM, so Table 5 does not establish the claimed memory limits of competing models. It also says all runs use torch.no_grad(), without explaining gradient re-enabling for conservative forces. The approximately 50-neighbor benchmark description conflicts with the proposed model’s 32-neighbor cap in Table 10 unless overridden. These issues require corrected failure classifications and explicit, matched execution settings.

Accuracy comparisons are confounded by training exposure. Appendix I states that the direct model receives 17 epochs of OMol25 pretraining before SPICE training, and the conservative model continues from that checkpoint. Equivalent baseline pretraining, dataset versions, split construction, overlap checks, and checkpoint selection are not sufficiently documented. Consequently, the SPICE improvements cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed architecture.

Significance and presentation—the headline efficiency claims exceed the evidence. For bounded neighbor count, existing O(NK) activations are already linear in N; the useful distinction is reduced dependence on K and elimination of large edge-feature tensors. Neighbor indices still require O(NK) storage. Figure 1’s 'Traditional EGNNs' curve is a synthetic gather implementation, not a representative full model, and the conclusion’s 20× inference acceleration generalizes a kernel comparison beyond the end-to-end results.

Physical validation is preliminary. Figure 4 and Appendix K omit the protein identity, experimental-reference details, timestep, thermostat settings, water trajectory duration, and replicate uncertainty. A single thermostatted trajectory with a high TM-score does not establish refinement or energy conservation. Absolute-coordinate factorization also needs an explanation of periodic images and numerical translation stability for these simulations.

Overall assessment: The practical direction is promising, but unresolved mathematical and implementation inconsistencies affect the central claims. Reproducibility is further limited by the blank code-release link and incomplete kernel/backward details. These are substantive evidential weaknesses requiring revision before acceptance.
